corrected_exact: action: Identify three separate paths: gravity loads the roof supports, wind acts on fabric and frame, and guyline tension transfers to anchors. The actual path depends on the shelter design. @E16,ED

corrected_exact: action: Check joints, anchors and line routing against the shelter instructions. A taut panel cannot establish load capacity. @E20,ED

corrected_exact: stop: If supports shift, split or deform or the shelter tears, leave the hazard area. Keep people out until a competent assessment. @E16,ED

corrected_exact: action: Use shelter-maker instructions for anchor type, placement and orientation. Saturated, soft or changing ground requires a different site when anchors cannot be secured. Follow site rules for any disturbance. @E20,E21,ED

original_exact: action: Test anchor firmness gently by hand before relying on the pitch and recheck anchors after rain saturates the soil or afternoon sun softens snowpack. @E16,E04,E20
corrected_exact: action: Inspect for movement after setup and weather changes. A gentle hand check can reveal a loose stake but cannot establish capacity in gusts. @E16,E20,ED

original_exact: stop: Never occupy an improvised roof that sags, creaks, shifts or accumulates snow; move immediately to clear ground, maintain wind/ground protection and seek help. @E05,E13,T06
corrected_exact: stop: Keep people out from under improvised roofs of unknown capacity. Sagging, movement or added wet debris are further reasons to leave the area immediately. @E13,E16,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize there is NO universally safe fire-to-shelter clearance distance: wind eddies, dry brush, synthetic fabric melting, sparks and radiant heat vary at every site. @C02,C18,ED
corrected_exact: action: Follow minimum clearances set by the site and product. Even when minimums are met, wind, sparks, combustibles and shelter materials can make outdoor placement unsafe. @C02,C05,ED

original_exact: stop: Extinguish or relocate an outdoor fire immediately if smoke enters the shelter, wind shifts toward dry materials or radiant heat warms shelter surfaces; never burn fuel inside an enclosure. @C02,C04,C05,C16
corrected_exact: stop: Use an established alternate shelter or the no-fire plan if safe separation is uncertain. Keep combustion out of shelters and vestibules. If CO is suspected, move to fresh air and call emergency services. @C05,C07,C08

original_exact: action: Without proper snow tools, formal training and an unobstructed escape plan, never roof over an excavated trench; use a low open windwall and insulated bed or existing refuge instead. @E05,E25,ED
corrected_exact: action: Avoid roofed excavations in this guide. Use stable surface shelter and insulation or an established refuge. Tools or training alone do not establish roof capacity at a specific site. @E23,E25,ED

original_exact: stop: Cracking, settling, dripping thaw, blocked drift exits or advancing hypothermia requires vacating any snow excavation immediately and moving to safer surface cover or rescue. @E06,E25,T03
corrected_exact: stop: Leave if an excavation shows movement, drift affects exit, or exposure worsens. Get to safer ground without entering runout terrain and seek help. @E23,E25,T06

original_exact: action: Exclude avalanche runouts, steep snow drifts and cornices entirely; keep digging tools inside with occupants only under trained protocols and maintain continuous external visibility/markers. @E23,E25,ED
corrected_exact: action: Avoid avalanche runouts, unstable snow and cornices. Treat this as hazard recognition; do not enter, excavate or test an overhead snow cavity using the diagram. @E23,E25,ED

original_exact: stop: Ceiling sag, cracking sounds, stuffy air, drowsiness, headache or drifting exit blockage demands immediate exit to fresh air and safer shelter. @C07,E25,T03
corrected_exact: stop: Exit immediately to fresh air and safer shelter if collapse, an obstructed exit or poor air is suspected. Seek emergency help for symptoms of CO exposure or serious cold illness. @E23,C07,T03

corrected_exact: diagram: Roof can fail without warning | Drift can block exit and air | Use stable surface refuge

original_exact: action: Check whether the filter uses an absolute pore rating (typically ≤1 micron for cysts and ~0.1–0.2 micron for bacteria) or only an unverified nominal rating. @W04,W19,W20,W21
corrected_exact: action: Identify the exact model and treatment claim. Nominal and absolute pore ratings differ. Product certification or test evidence must cover the organism of concern. @W04,W20,W21

original_exact: action: Select boiling or a filter explicitly certified for cyst reduction (absolute pore size ≤1 micron or NSF/ANSI Standard 53/55) to remove parasites reliably. @W19,W20,W02
corrected_exact: action: Use boiling or a filter independently certified for cyst reduction or removal, or rated at one micron absolute or smaller for parasite reduction. Look for a cyst-specific claim under NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 where certified. @W20

corrected_exact: diagram: Routine chlorine misses Crypto | Verify specific cyst claim | Boil when appropriate

corrected_exact: visual: Compares parasite barriers. Neither a standard number by itself nor cyst removal establishes protection against all hazards.

original_exact: action: Shake and blow or drain excess water gently per manufacturer instructions immediately after filtering, remembering that microscopic pores remain damp. @W28,ED
corrected_exact: action: Read the exact model instructions for draining and storage. A cartridge that looks drained can still contain water. @W28

original_exact: action: Keep the damp cartridge sealed in a waterproof bag inside your inner clothing during travel and inside your sleeping bag overnight whenever temperatures approach freezing. @W28,E10
corrected_exact: action: Protect the wetted filter against freezing as the manufacturer directs. Maintain a treatment backup for water within its limits. @W28,W02

original_exact: stop: Any wet filter left out in freezing air is compromised—stop relying on it for microbial safety and use boiling or another verified supply. @W28,W02
corrected_exact: stop: If a wetted filter might have frozen, stop relying on it and follow the model instructions for replacement or an approved integrity check. Use a supported alternate treatment or carried potable water. @W28,W02

original_exact: action: Confirm the bottle is plain unscented liquid bleach with 5%–9% sodium hypochlorite—never use scented, color-safe, splash-less or cleaner-added bleach. @W12
corrected_exact: action: Prefer an approved safe supply or boiling when appropriate. Use bleach only as an emergency option and only if the product and concentration are covered by a current official instruction. @W01,W02,W12

original_exact: action: Clarify cloudy water first, measure the label-matched EPA/CDC dose (for 5%–9% bleach: about 8 drops or just under 1/8 tsp per gallon of clear water; double if still slightly cloudy), and mix thoroughly. @W12,W08
corrected_exact: action: Follow local public health directions or one complete current EPA or CDC protocol. Verify the exact formulation, water volume and required pretreatment. Do not combine tables or improvise a rounded dose. @W12

original_exact: action: Let stand at least 30 minutes; water should have a faint chlorine odor (if not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes), remembering chlorine does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium. @W12,W20
corrected_exact: action: Follow the selected protocol for the full dose and contact time. A chlorine smell alone cannot prove treatment, and this process does not reliably address all parasites. @W12,W20

original_exact: verify: Confirm bleach label concentration, exact volume dosed, 30-minute timer completion and faint chlorine smell before drinking. @W12,ED
corrected_exact: verify: Record the source protocol, product concentration, water volume, exact dose and elapsed time. @W12,ED

original_exact: stop: Reject bleach disinfection if chemical/fuel/algal contamination is suspected, if bleach concentration is unreadable or non-plain, or if Cryptosporidium risk requires boiling or cyst filtration. @W01,W12,W15,W20
corrected_exact: stop: Use another supply if the product strength or treatment steps are uncertain, or if a chemical, fuel or algal toxin hazard is suspected. @W01,W12,W15

original_exact: diagram: Verify 5-9% unscented label | Clarify and dose per gallon | Mix and wait ≥30 min
corrected_exact: diagram: Confirm product and concentration | Follow one official table | Record dose and contact time

original_exact: visual: Mechanism diagram tracing chlorine concentration verification, turbidity pre-clarification and 30-minute contact-time inactivation kinetics. Conceptual, not to scale.
corrected_exact: visual: Protocol-selection schematic. Select the applicable local or agency instructions for the entire procedure.

original_exact: action: Clarify turbid water first and extend contact time strictly according to the label when treating cold water or targeting resistant parasites like Cryptosporidium. @W05,W08,W20
corrected_exact: action: Follow the exact product instructions for water clarity, temperature, volume and contact time. If the product does not claim efficacy for the expected pathogen under those conditions, select a suitable treatment or verified supply. @W04,W05,W20

original_exact: action: Reject chemical disinfection if bleach is older than recommended or lacks a faint chlorine odor after repeat dosing, or if tablets are expired, damp or crumbled. @W12,W05
corrected_exact: action: Reject unlabeled, expired or contaminated reagents and any batch that did not meet its official time and dose requirements. Odor cannot verify microbial safety. @W05,W12

original_exact: action: Brace the tip of the ferrocerium rod firmly on a stable surface right beside the dry tinder bundle—stabilizing the rod prevents knocking the tinder apart mid-strike. @C11,C03,ED
corrected_exact: action: Identify the rod, compatible striker and suitable dry tinder from the model instructions. Inspect tool control cold before any authorized live use. @C03,C11,ED

original_exact: action: Scrape firmly along the rod with a sharp square-spined striker (or pull the rod back cleanly against a stationary striker) to shave hot oxidizing ferrocerium particles directly onto fine tinder. @C11,C03,ED
corrected_exact: action: Ferrocerium and traditional flint-and-steel produce hot particles from different materials. Follow the product instructions for any live training. @C10,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize that traditional flint-and-steel sheds tiny particles of carbon STEEL shaved off by a hard rock edge (flint/chert), producing cooler short-lived sparks that require charred cloth or specialized punkwood to catch an ember. @C10
corrected_exact: action: In traditional flint-and-steel, a hard stone edge removes small steel particles. A compatible dry receiver, such as prepared char cloth used in the NPS demonstration, can catch them. @C10

original_exact: action: Recognize that a modern ferrocerium rod sheds engineered pyrophoric alloy shavings that burn far hotter and longer, able to ignite fine dry fibrous tinder or commercial tabs directly. @C10,C11,ED
corrected_exact: action: Modern ferrocerium equipment differs in material and compatible striker. Use exact product instructions; this comparison does not establish relative spark temperature, duration or wet performance. @C10,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize that upright isobutane/propane canisters are simple and have an on/off shutoff valve (often permitted under Stage 1/2 fire restrictions where open fires are banned), yet lose pressure sharply in freezing cold unless inverted/regulated per manufacturer design. @C13,C15,ED
corrected_exact: action: Check the local order for the exact stove type and permitted operation. A shutoff valve alone does not establish permission. Check the model temperature and fuel limits. @C13,C15,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize that pumped liquid-fuel stoves maintain strong output in subfreezing temperatures and high elevation, yet require careful outdoor priming, leak checks and manufacturer-matched fuel. @C15,ED
corrected_exact: action: Match fuel and operating conditions to the stove instructions. This comparison does not establish that a given liquid-fuel stove will perform safely at a particular altitude or temperature. @C15,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize that solid-fuel tablet or alcohol stoves lack an instant shutoff valve, are frequently prohibited during Stage 1/2 fire restrictions and burn weakly in wind without careful shielding. @C13,C15,ED
corrected_exact: action: Check whether the exact solid-fuel or alcohol appliance is permitted. If legality or operation is uncertain, choose a no-fire alternative. @C13,C08,ED

original_exact: action: Follow the exact manufacturer instructions for windscreen clearance and remote-canister routing; use a natural rock or pack windblock set well back instead of trapping heat around canisters. @C15,ED
corrected_exact: action: Follow the exact model instructions. Some canister-top stoves explicitly prohibit all windscreens. Do not add or position a barrier that the instructions prohibit or that can redirect heat toward the fuel container. @C15,C21

original_exact: stop: Shut off the stove immediately if the fuel canister grows noticeably warm, flames lick around the tank or pot supports wobble. @C15,C05
corrected_exact: stop: If fuel heating, abnormal flames or unstable supports are suspected, stop use and follow the manufacturer emergency guidance. If you cannot safely shut it down, move away and seek help. @C21,T01,T02

original_exact: action: Recognize that high elevation lowers available oxygen and cold cooking pots quench flames, increasing incomplete combustion and CO output from camping stoves and heaters. @C05,C16
corrected_exact: action: Cold, altitude, appliance design and pot placement can affect combustion; appearance and altitude do not establish a safe CO output. Use camping stoves outdoors and follow the exact model limits. @C16,C21

original_exact: failure: Assuming a clean blue propane flame inside an open-sided snow pit or partly open garage produces no dangerous carbon monoxide. @C05,C16,C07
corrected_exact: failure: Treating an open vestibule or a blue flame as proof that exhaust cannot accumulate around people. @C05,C16

original_exact: action: Observe how the downed log rests on the ground before touching the saw: a log supported at both ends sags in the middle (compression on top, tension on bottom), whereas a cantilevered overhanging end compresses on the bottom and pulls apart on top. @K05
corrected_exact: action: Assess supports, slope and visible movement before touching the saw. A simple support sketch only indicates one possible load case; hidden constraints and decay can change the bind. @K05,ED

original_exact: action: Make a shallow relief cut on the compression side first if needed, or cut from the tension-relieved side while watching the kerf—if the saw slot begins closing, STOP and relieve bind from the opposite side or reposition the support. @K05,ED
corrected_exact: action: Leave cuts requiring bind relief, support changes or work on loaded timber to trained sawyers. If the kerf closes or wood moves, stop and clear the drop or roll area. @K05,K10

original_exact: diagram: Compression closes saw kerf | Tension pulls kerf open | Cut safely clear of drop zone
corrected_exact: diagram: Inspect supports from clear ground | Closing kerf signals bind | Stop and clear movement path

corrected_exact: visual: Hazard-recognition schematic. No relief-cut sequence or work under stored load is shown.

original_exact: action: Prefer splitting small straight knot-free wood (wrist diameter or smaller) using wooden wedges driven by a stout deadwood mallet once a shallow starter split opens. @K12,K06,K03
corrected_exact: action: Prefer small prepared fuel or a purpose-designed splitting tool used as directed on a stable work surface. Avoid knotty, twisted or stressed stock. @K01,K08,ED

original_exact: action: If batoning small straight deadwood with a sturdy fixed-blade knife, strike ONLY on the blade spine near the tip with a smooth deadwood club (never steel or rock), stopping immediately if the blade hits a hard knot or starts twisting. @K02,K12,ED
corrected_exact: action: If a knife is not specifically rated by its maker for impact use, do not strike it. No improvised blade or club configuration is validated here. @K01,K02,ED

corrected_exact: stop: If a blade or wedge binds, stop applying force, clear the area and follow the tool maker or instructor for safe recovery. @K01,K02,ED

corrected_exact: Z09-P44 | Understand the force on a fixed pulley redirect | NPS Forces and Tools and USFS rigging boundaries; new manuscript

original_exact: action: Recognize that passing a rope over a single stationary limb or fixed pulley changes pulling direction (1:1 ideal advantage) while ACTUALLY DOUBLING the total downward load on the anchor (load plus pulling force) minus friction. @K06,K09
corrected_exact: action: A fixed pulley can redirect a line without ideal mechanical advantage. The anchor reaction comes from the vector sum of the segment pulls. Equal tensions give about twice a segment tension only when both segments pull in the same direction. @K13

original_exact: action: Recognize that high friction over a rough tree branch can cut usable lifting output in half while sawing straight through rope fibers and damaging tree bark. @K06,K09,K11
corrected_exact: action: A different rope angle changes the resultant. Friction can produce unequal tensions; shock loading and support geometry change the practical hazard. This diagram is a static model, not sizing guidance. @K13,ED

original_exact: action: Remember that compound pulley systems multiply tension on anchors rapidly—camp cordage, tree branches and improvised carabiners carry ZERO certified lifting or rescue ratings. @K06,K09
corrected_exact: action: Inspect the concept unloaded. Use rated and independently reviewed equipment and systems for actual lifting. Keep people out of the load path and overhead hazard area. @K09,K13,ED

original_exact: objective: Recognize how simple rope redirects change pull direction and multiply forces on the overhead anchor point.
corrected_exact: objective: Distinguish rope-segment tension from the anchor reaction in an ideal redirect.

original_exact: failure: Hauling a heavy gear sack over a dead brittle branch using a redirect without realizing the branch carries roughly double the bag weight plus friction pull. @K06,K09,E13
corrected_exact: failure: Assuming a redirect anchor only carries one line tension, or treating a two-times sketch as a safe working rating. @K13

original_exact: verify: Inspect the overhead anchor for soundness, keep bystanders completely out from underneath suspended utility loads and stay well within light camp loads. @K06,K09,K08,E13
corrected_exact: verify: In a diagram, identify both force directions and explain why their angle matters. @K13,ED

corrected_exact: diagram: Two rope pulls act on the pulley | Resultant depends on angle | No working-load rating

corrected_exact: visual: Free-body sketches show equal-tension parallel and right-angle examples under a static idealization.

original_exact: action: Check the geodetic datum printed in the map margin before plotting GPS points: modern US Topo sheets and GPS receivers default to WGS84 or NAD83 (virtually identical for foot travel), whereas older historical USGS sheets often use NAD27. @N01,N04
corrected_exact: action: Read the exact horizontal datum and coordinate format in the map margin and receiver. UTM is a grid system, not a datum. Confirm both before plotting. @N01,N11

original_exact: action: Recognize that plotting a WGS84 GPS coordinate straight onto an unadjusted NAD27 map grid can shift your plotted position by tens to hundreds of meters—enough to place you on the wrong side of a cliff or river. @N01,ED
corrected_exact: action: NAD27, NAD83 and WGS84 identifiers do not justify a guessed shift. Use an authoritative transformation when the reference frames differ; the displacement depends on location and reference. @N11

original_exact: action: Match your GPS receiver datum setting to the paper map's printed datum (or switch to a modern WGS84/NAD83 US Topo sheet) and always cross-check the plotted point against surrounding terrain contours. @N01,N03,ED
corrected_exact: action: Record datum, format and grid zone as applicable. Cross-check the transformed position against identifiable terrain before using it for movement. @N01,N11,ED

original_exact: action: Test for localized geologic magnetic anomalies (common in iron-rich northern bedrock) by walking twenty steps and sighting back toward your starting point—if the reverse bearing disagrees sharply from 180 degrees opposite, local rock is deflecting the needle. @N08,ED
corrected_exact: action: If reciprocal bearings disagree, recheck observation technique, equipment and nearby interference. The mismatch alone cannot identify the cause or establish a safe route. @N08,ED

original_exact: action: Lay the compass edge on the mapped landmark aligned with map north and trace back along the edge until it intersects your known trail or ridge—that intersection marks your approximate position. @N08,N03,ED
corrected_exact: action: Use the correct map reference for the bearing. From the plotted landmark, draw the reciprocal direction back toward your known linear feature. Treat their crossing as a candidate location and compare it with the terrain. @N03,T08,ED

original_exact: action: Identify two (ideally three) unmistakable mapped landmarks separated by a wide angular spread (roughly 60 to 120 degrees apart) rather than clustered close together. @N03,N08
corrected_exact: action: Use unmistakable mapped landmarks in substantially different directions. Near-parallel bearings make an approximate intersection less useful. @N03,ED

original_exact: action: Recognize that **406 MHz Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs)** require NO subscription, transmit high-power distress alerts directly to NOAA SARSAT satellites and carry a local 121.5 MHz homing beacon—yet are ONE-WAY distress-only devices for grave and imminent danger. @N05
corrected_exact: action: A registered 406 MHz PLB sends a distress alert through the Cospas-Sarsat system. Check the beacon model for homing or return-link features. A return-link indication is not a two-way conversation or a guarantee of rescue. @N05,N12

original_exact: action: Register every 406 MHz PLB with NOAA SARSAT immediately upon purchase (required by federal law, free of charge) and update emergency contacts, medical notes and trip details whenever they change or at least every two years. @N05
corrected_exact: action: Register a U.S.-coded beacon with NOAA, update changed information and verify registration at least every two years. Check the relevant authority for other country codes. @N12

original_exact: stop: Reserve 406 MHz PLB activation strictly for grave and imminent life-safety emergencies—if accidentally triggered, shut it off immediately and notify NOAA SARSAT / rescue authorities to cancel false dispatch. @N05
corrected_exact: stop: For an accidental activation, turn the beacon off and contact the appropriate rescue coordination center immediately with the beacon ID. Use the current NOAA false-alert instructions. @N12

original_exact: action: Move the entire group together to the upwind edge of a clear open space away from dead snags, powerlines and loose branches; crouch low protecting eyes from blowing grit/snow and stay put until flight crew explicitly wave you forward. @N09,E13,T01,ED
corrected_exact: action: Wait clear of the aircraft where dispatch or the crew directs. Secure loose gear from a safe position before its arrival, and keep the group together. @N13,ED

original_exact: action: Never approach a helicopter from uphill (spinning main rotor dips dangerously low) or anywhere near the rear tail rotor—approach ONLY from the front/side within the pilot's direct sight when signaled by crew. @T01,N09,ED
corrected_exact: action: Do not approach or enter a landing area without explicit crew direction. Crew instructions determine the approach, if any; improvised approach rules are not a substitute. @N13,ED

original_exact: diagram: Stow ALL loose fabric/gear | Wait clear of snags & wires | Approach ONLY when crew signals
corrected_exact: diagram: Secure loose gear from safety | Wait clear of aircraft | Follow the crew only

original_exact: visual: Environmental helicopter/ground-extraction safety zone marking stowed-gear boundary, tail-rotor/uphill exclusion zones and crew-directed approach corridor. Conceptual, not to scale.
corrected_exact: visual: Waiting-site priorities. This is not a landing-zone or aircraft approach diagram.

original_exact: action: Offer ONLY low-risk shore-based assistance (extending a long branch, throwing a float/rope from firm ground, lowering dry warm clothing if safely anchored)—never climb unroped down slick cliffs or walk out onto broken ice. @T01,X18,K09
corrected_exact: action: From stable land, offer reach or throw assistance only if it can be done safely. Stop if you could be pulled in or need to approach the hazard. Follow dispatcher directions. @X20,T02

original_exact: action: Reject three classic false social signs: (4) "there are footprints or dog tracks ahead" (lighter weight or earlier colder morning), (5) "a snowmobile crossed fast" (speed skims thin spots that break under slow boots), and (6) "other people are out there" (others may be in unseen danger or over a different safe pocket). @X01,E12
corrected_exact: action: Reject tracks, observed crossings and other traffic as evidence that your location is safe. Loads and conditions differ and ice strength can vary over short distances. @X01,E12

original_exact: action: **First ~1 minute (Cold Shock):** Sudden cold immersion triggers an involuntary gasp reflex, rapid uncontrolled hyperventilation and blood-pressure spike—without a fastened life jacket keeping your mouth above water, inhaling water causes immediate drowning. @X02,X03,X04
corrected_exact: action: Cold shock can begin immediately with gasp and rapid breathing. Protect the airway and use available flotation while breathing settles enough to act. @X02,X03,X04

original_exact: action: **First ~10 minutes (Cold Incapacitation / Swim Failure):** Frigid water cools arm and leg nerves and muscles rapidly, destroying finger grip and swimming power long before core hypothermia occurs—use these minutes to self-exit or secure flotation/rescue rather than attempting a long swim. @X02,X03
corrected_exact: action: Cold can quickly reduce grip, movement and swimming ability. Take a safe opportunity for exit or flotation early; do not budget a fixed window for action. @X02,X03

original_exact: action: **Roughly 1 hour+ (Core Hypothermia):** Core body temperature drops progressively over tens of minutes to an hour or more depending on clothing, size and water temperature—if trapped in water with flotation, minimize movement and conserve heat while awaiting rescue. @X02,X03
corrected_exact: action: Core cooling and survival vary widely with water, clothing, flotation and the person. The 1–10–1 mnemonic describes phases, not deadlines or a promised survival time. @X03

original_exact: stop: Treat ANY immersion in water below 70°F (especially below 50°F) as a time-critical drowning and hypothermia emergency requiring immediate 911/USCG activation. @X02,X03,T02
corrected_exact: stop: Respond to a cold-water emergency promptly. Keep the airway above water, signal for help and follow emergency guidance. Do not wait for a temperature or time threshold. @X02,X03,T02

original_exact: diagram: ~1 min: control cold-shock gasp | ~10 min: exit/secure before swim fails | ~1 hr+: conserve heat w/ PFD
corrected_exact: diagram: Cold shock can be immediate | Movement can deteriorate quickly | Core cooling varies

original_exact: visual: Mechanism timeline mapping the 1-10-1 cold-water immersion phases (cold shock, swim failure, core hypothermia) to time-critical survival actions. Conceptual, not to scale.
corrected_exact: visual: Conceptual phases with no fixed onset, swimming capability or survival window.

original_exact: action: Control breathing first during the initial 1-minute cold-shock gasp—keep your airway clear above the rim, resist flailing wildly and turn back toward the direction you came from (where ice already held your weight). @X02,X03,X18
corrected_exact: action: Protect your airway and regain breathing control as able. If possible, face the direction you came from, which was the last route to support you. It is not guaranteed safe ice. @X19

original_exact: action: Place arms flat on the solid shelf edge (planting ice picks if carried), kick your legs vigorously to bring your body horizontal like swimming and pull/slide forward onto the ice—if the rim breaks, keep working back toward thicker ice. @X18,X03
corrected_exact: action: If able to self-exit, get your body horizontal and kick while using the edge or ice picks to pull forward. Avoid any promise that a particular edge will support you. @X19

original_exact: stop: If unable to exit within functional minutes, hook arms/coat sleeves onto the ice edge if freezing in place, blow whistle/shout and preserve airway while awaiting emergency rescue (specialist review pending). @X18,X03,T02
corrected_exact: stop: If unable to get out, signal for rescue and prioritize keeping your airway clear. Do not wait for a fixed number of minutes or rely on clothing freezing to the ice as a planned technique. @X19,X03

original_exact: action: Talk calmly to help the victim control cold-shock breathing and turn toward thicker ice while you stay low and anchored on firm ground (or secured shore edge) extending a long branch, sled, ladder or throwing a buoyant rescue line/jug. @X18,X02,T01
corrected_exact: action: From stable shore, reassure the person and offer a reach or throw aid only if it can be done safely without entering the hazard. @X20

original_exact: action: Brace yourself low on shore before pulling so a sudden jerk cannot drag you into the water; if no safe reach or throw reaches the victim, stay alive on shore, keep visual contact and guide arriving fire/ice rescue teams. @X18,T01,T02
corrected_exact: action: Let go of a reach aid if you are being pulled in. If safe help is out of reach, remain on shore and report the person’s position to responders. @X20,T02

original_exact: stop: Never enter the water or step onto unsupported broken ice without specialized rescue training, exposure suit and tethered professional backup. @X18,T01
corrected_exact: stop: Stay on land. Do not enter the water or go onto ice to perform an improvised rescue. @X20,T01

original_exact: stop: Continue active cooling until EMS takes over or the person becomes fully alert and shivering—follow 911 dispatcher directions strictly for breathing/CPR changes. @T05,T09,T02
